description: Data Comet is a team of data and web enthusiasts passionate about space. We combine Python, data analysis, dashboards and web design to turn complex data into clear, interactive tools. We want to apply these skills to real NASA data at Space Apps Algiers 2026.
summary:
FlameX is a web platform that turns NASA's research on fire in microgravity into something people can actually use. NASA has run dozens of combustion experiments in space, but the results are spread across reports, spreadsheets and even handwritten test sheets, which makes them hard to use when designing a new habitat.

We gathered 24 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics system, extracted their test data, and built a backend that can answer questions with citations, predict how a fuel droplet burns under different cabin air, and rank which studies matter most for a given habitat.

On top of that we built three dashboards. Researchers get the full prediction model, a map of where NASA's data runs out, suggestions for the next experiment, and a tool to screen materials. Engineers get a scenario planner to see how changing a habitat's oxygen or pressure changes fire risk. Students get a simple playground and explanations of why flames are round in space.

This matters because the Moon and Mars bases NASA is considering would use oxygen-rich, low-pressure air that has barely been tested, and a fire there leaves no room for guesswork.
details:
FlameX has two parts: a data backend we call FlameAtlas, and a web app on top of it. For the backend, we collected the documents and tables from 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations, including FLEX, SAFFIRE-II, BASS and the ACME series. Some of the most useful data, ACME test sheets, existed only as handwritten scans, so we used Claude's vision model to read them into structured rows. Every extracted row keeps a link to the page it came from. From this we built four things:

a searchable index that answers questions in plain language, cites the exact NASA passage behind each sentence, and runs a second check that removes any sentence the sources don't support:

a knowledge graph linking investigations, materials, gases and findings , which helps with questions like "which fuels were tested with both CO₂ and helium?

a prediction model trained on the FLEX and CFI droplet tests from the ISS. Given a fuel, oxygen level, pressure and added CO₂ or helium, it predicts how much of the droplet burns, with a 90 % range and a warning when the conditions are far from any real test.

a ranking method (AHP weights combined with OWA aggregation) that scores each investigation for a given habitat and the user's priorities.

The web app splits users by role, chosen once at sign-up:

Users get the flame simulator with all its controls.

Reaserchers get a flammability map showing where NASA's tests stop, a test-gap finder that suggests the next most useful experiment, and a material screening tool. You upload a CSV of materials, and each one is matched to what NASA actually burned and checked against every habitat's oxygen level.

Engineers get fire-control cards (prevention, detection, suppression) and a what-if planner. You start from a habitat's real air, change it with a slider or a sentence like "Mars base raises oxygen to 30 %", and see the fire risk for each fuel before and after, plus how the relevant studies re-rank.

Students get a playground with one oxygen slider and an answer in plain words, illustrated fire basics, a history of space fire incidents, and how this research helps on Earth.

Benefits:

Hours of reading become seconds. Finding what NASA knows about a material or an atmosphere takes seconds, with the source one click away.

Gaps are visible. The app shows where the evidence is thin instead of hiding it. Moon and Mars conditions are clearly marked as extrapolations, and the habitat atmospheres NASA hasn't confirmed are labelled as assumptions.

Experiments get better targets. It helps choose which experiment to run next, which matters when every test in orbit costs crew time.

One source, three audiences. The same verified data serves researchers, engineers and students, each at the right level.

AI costs stay low. The simulator, maps and rankings run without AI calls. AI is used only when someone asks a question or types a scenario, and answers are cached.

Intended impact:

We want FlameX to support decisions about future habitats: which cabin atmosphere to choose, which materials to fly, and which fire tests to run before people live on the Moon or Mars. We also want it to be a way in for students, because most of the energy we use on Earth still comes from combustion, and space research helps make it cleaner and safer.

Limits we are open about:

The model only covers liquid droplet flames tested in microgravity. It doesn't predict solid materials, gas leaks or large fires, and it can't account for Moon or Mars gravity, because NASA's PSI data has no partial-gravity tests yet.

The material screening is a first filter, not a replacement for NASA's standard flammability tests.

Tools and technologies:

Languages: Python, JavaScript (React), HTML and CSS

Backend: FastAPI, ChromaDB, MiniLM embeddings, TF-IDF and a reranker for hybrid search, pandas

AI: Claude (Anthropic) for cited answers, fact-checking, data extraction, reading handwritten scans, and parsing what-if sentences

Modelling and ranking: a droplet-flame prediction model with uncertainty ranges, plus AHP and OWA multi-criteria ranking

Frontend: React 18, Vite, d3-geo and topojson for the 3D globes, SVG charts we built ourselves, and a custom design system with dark and light themes

Data: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) and the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS)

Collaboration: GitHub, ngrok for sharing the backend during development

Hardware: none.
